content:
Critics sometimes say that Muslims make Muhammad ﷺ a second object of devotion. They point to the salutations after his name, the poems in his praise and the love that Muslims openly show him.

The charge deserves a careful answer, because the love is real and Muslims make no secret of it. They name their sons after him in every generation, recite poems in his honour, weep at his grave in Medina, and treat any insult to him as an insult to themselves. To an outsider, especially one from a tradition that worships a man as God, that can look like worship. The question is what Islam itself counts as worship, and whether any of it is directed to him.

The earliest texts answer the charge in the Prophet's own words and in the words of the Companions. These seven points set out what they say.

The Prophet is told to say: "I am only a man like you, to whom it is revealed that your god is one God" (18:110). He is also told to say that he has no power over benefit or harm for himself except what God wills (7:188). The Quran puts a similar limit on his status in 3:144: "Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him."[1]

The statement of faith repeats the point. A Muslim says that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His servant (abd) and messenger, and the word servant comes first.

Other verses draw the same line in the Prophet's own voice. When his opponents demanded that he make springs gush from the earth or climb into the sky, he was told to answer, "Glory to my Lord, am I anything but a human messenger?" He was also told to say that he did not claim to hold the treasures of God, nor to know the unseen, nor to be an angel.[2] A founder who wanted to be worshipped would not have recited those verses to his own followers.

The strongest form of the objection points to intercession: Muslims hope for the Prophet's intercession on the Day of Judgement, and some call on him by name. The Quran says that no one intercedes with God except by His permission, and the hadith of intercession describe the Prophet prostrating before God and asking leave to speak.[3] Muslims have long argued among themselves about calling on him after his death, but every party to that argument denies that he is divine or that he acts by his own power.

The Quran tells the believers to send blessings upon him (33:56) and to lower their voices in his presence (49:2). It makes obedience to him part of obedience to God (4:80) and ties love of God to following him (3:31).[4] Muslim reverence for the Prophet therefore rests on a command of God and does not originate in a human tradition.

The same book that tells them to honour him also tells him to call himself a man. The two instructions have to be read together, and the early Muslims did read them together.

The form of the blessing itself answers the charge. When a Muslim says salla Allahu alayhi wa sallam, he is asking God to bless the Prophet and grant him peace. The prayer is addressed to God, on behalf of the Prophet, which is the opposite of praying to him. Every time the salutation follows his name, it repeats that he is a recipient of God's grace.

A verse in Surat al-Fath shows the same order. The believers are to believe in God and His Messenger, to support him and honour him, and to glorify Him morning and evening.[5] The commentators explained that the honour belongs to the Messenger and the glorification, tasbih, belongs to God alone. The Quran gives each its due in a single sentence.

Umar reports from the pulpit that he heard the Prophet say: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated about the son of Mary. I am only His servant, so say servant of God and His messenger."[6]

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani explains itra as praise that goes beyond the truth, and says that the comparison refers to the Christian claim of divinity for Jesus.[7] The Prophet named the boundary and told his community where it lay.

He enforced it when Companions crossed it. Mu'adh ibn Jabal returned from Syria, where he had seen people prostrate to their bishops and leaders, and prostrated to the Prophet. The Prophet asked him what he was doing, and told him not to do it, saying that if he were to command anyone to prostrate to another, he would have commanded a wife to prostrate to her husband.[8] The point of the saying is that prostration belongs to God, so no human being, the Prophet included, may receive it.

When a man said to him, "What God wills and what you will", the Prophet answered, "Have you made me an equal to God? Say: what God alone wills."[9] He corrected the phrase although it was meant as courtesy, because it put his will beside God's.

When the Prophet's son Ibrahim died, the sun was eclipsed, and some people said that the eclipse had come because of the death. According to al-Mughira ibn Shuba, the Prophet answered that the sun and moon do not eclipse for anyone's death or birth, and he told the people to pray and to call on God.[10]

A man who wanted to be worshipped had every reason to accept the claim. He rejected it on the day of his own bereavement.

The same report was transmitted by several Companions, among them A'isha and Abu Bakra, and in their accounts the Prophet led the people in a long prayer of the eclipse and then preached to them that the sun and moon are two of the signs of God.[11] He turned an event that people wanted to read as a sign of his importance into an occasion of worship of God.

Muslims do report miracles at his hands, as the Quran does of earlier prophets. The Quran attributes every such sign to God, and tells the Prophet to say that signs are with God alone.[12] A miracle in Islam is evidence that God has sent a messenger, and the credit for it goes to God.

Aisha and Ibn Abbas report that near the end of his life the Prophet kept pulling a cloth over his face. When he felt short of breath he uncovered it and said that God had cursed the Jews and the Christians for making the graves of their prophets places of worship. They add that he was warning his community against what they had done.[13]

The warning concerned his own grave, at a time when he knew he was dying.

Other reports carry the same warning in his own words. Abu Dawud records that he said, "Do not make your houses graves, and do not make my grave a place of festival, and send blessings upon me, for your blessings reach me wherever you are."[14] Malik records that he prayed, "O God, do not make my grave an idol that is worshipped."[15]

The strongest form of the objection points to the crowds at his mosque in Medina and the green dome over his grave. Muslims visit the mosque to pray in it, and greet the Prophet at his grave as they greet any of the dead. Scholars have argued for centuries over what that visit may include, with Ibn Taymiyya and Taqi al-Din al-Subki taking opposite sides in the fourteenth century.[16] Both men held that worship belongs to God alone. Their dispute was over etiquette and travel, and neither of them proposed praying to the Prophet.

When the Prophet died, Umar stood and declared that he had not died. Abu Bakr arrived from al-Sunh, uncovered the Prophet's face and kissed it, and then addressed the crowd: whoever worshipped Muhammad should know that Muhammad is dead, and whoever worships God should know that God is living and never dies. He then recited the verse of Al Imran, "Muhammad is only a messenger" (3:144).[17]

Umar sat down when Abu Bakr spoke. The community then chose a successor to a man it had just confirmed to be mortal.

Umar later described the effect of that moment. When he heard Abu Bakr recite the verse, he said, it was as if he had never heard it before, and his legs could no longer carry him, and he sank to the ground knowing that the Prophet had died.[18] The most devoted of the Companions accepted the verdict of the Quran over his own grief.

The sentence of Abu Bakr has become the standard Muslim answer to the charge in this article. It separates the man from the God he served, and it was spoken by the man who had been closest to him for twenty-three years, beside his body, before any later theology could shape it.

Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet said he would be the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, the first to rise from the grave, the first to intercede and the first whose intercession is accepted.[19] The same Abu Hurayra reports in al-Bukhari that he said no one should say that he is better than Yunus ibn Matta.[20]

The first report describes a rank that God gave. The second stops a believer from using that rank to belittle another prophet. Honour for Muhammad in Islam sits inside honour for all the messengers.

Other versions add two words that show the spirit of the report. In al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet says that he will be the master of the children of Adam "and no boast", and that the banner of praise will be in his hand "and no boast".[21] He also told his Companions not to prefer him over Moses, describing how on the Day of Resurrection he would find Moses already holding the side of the Throne.[22]

The Quran tells Muslims to make no distinction between any of the messengers in believing in them.[23] Muslims hold that God has raised some above others, and that Muhammad is the last and the highest. They also hold that every one of them was a servant of God, and that none of them is to be worshipped.

The bottom line

The sources describe a Prophet who accepted a rank and refused devotion. The Quran calls him a servant, the Prophet rejected exaggerated praise, and Abu Bakr gave the answer to the charge on the day of the death. A Muslim who loves him and blesses him is following a command of the Quran, and one who treats him as divine is breaking the same text.

What Muslims do give him is love, obedience and imitation. They pray as he prayed, fast as he fasted, and try to speak and eat and treat their families as he did, because the Quran calls him a beautiful example for anyone who hopes in God.[24] That is how a follower honours a teacher. The prayer, the prostration, the fasting and the hope of the believer are all directed to the One whom the Prophet himself worshipped.

Notes

  1. Quran 18:110, 7:188 and 3:144.
  2. Quran 17:90–93; 6:50.
  3. Quran 2:255; 20:109; Sahih al-Bukhari 7510, Book of Tawhid, the hadith of intercession reported by Anas ibn Malik.
  4. Quran 33:56, 49:2, 4:80 and 3:31.
  5. Quran 48:8–9.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 3445 (Book of the Prophets, chapter on the verse "And mention in the Book, Maryam"), narrated by Umar from the pulpit; see Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 478.
  7. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, vol. 6, p. 490, in the chapter on the descent of Jesus, son of Mary, where he explains la tutruni and itra.
  8. Sunan Ibn Majah 1853, Book of Marriage, report of Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa on Mu'adh ibn Jabal.
  9. Musnad Ahmad, report of Ibn Abbas; compare al-Nasa'i, al-Sunan al-Kubra, Book of the Day and Night.
  10. Sahih al-Bukhari 1043 (Book of the Eclipses), narrated by al-Mughira ibn Shuba.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 1044 (report of A'isha) and 1040 (report of Abu Bakra), Book of the Eclipses.
  12. Quran 6:109; 29:50.
  13. Sahih al-Bukhari 435 and 436 (Book of Prayer), narrated by Aisha and Abdullah ibn Abbas.
  14. Sunan Abi Dawud 2042, Book of Rites, report of Abu Hurayra.
  15. Malik ibn Anas, al-Muwatta, Book of the Shortening of the Prayer, report of Ata ibn Yasar (mursal).
  16. Ibn Taymiyya, al-Radd ala al-Ikhna'i; Taqi al-Din al-Subki, Shifa al-Siqam fi Ziyarat Khayr al-Anam.
  17. Sahih al-Bukhari 3667 and 3668 (Book of the Companions of the Prophet), narrated by Aisha; see Fath al-Bari, vol. 7, p. 19.
  18. Sahih al-Bukhari 4454, Book of Military Expeditions, chapter on the illness and death of the Prophet.
  19. Sahih Muslim 2278 (Book of Virtues, chapter on the superiority of our Prophet over all creation), narrated by Abu Hurayra.
  20. Sahih al-Bukhari 3416 (Book of the Prophets, chapter on the verse "And verily, Yunus was one of the messengers"), narrated by Abu Hurayra.
  21. Jami al-Tirmidhi 3148, Book of Commentary, report of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.
  22. Sahih al-Bukhari 2411, Book of Disputes, report of Abu Hurayra.
  23. Quran 2:285; compare 2:253.
  24. Quran 33:21.
